1.3:
Let's first find out the conditions for parameters (a,b,c,d), under which the functions represent a perturbation propagating at a constant velocity while maintaining its shape. The variables z and t and the parameters (a,b,c,d) were assumed real. The parameters (a,b,c,d) were further assumed to not depend on time t or location z.

I: ψ (z,t)=exp[-(a²z²+b²t²-2abtz+c)] = exp(-(az-bt)²-c) = exp[-a²(z-(b)/(a)t)²-c]

a) The function propagates at a constant velocity while maintaining its shape if a,b ≠ 0. This can be seen from the form of the equation which resembles the form of eq. (3.1.1) in the lecture notes (i.e. ψ (z,t) = f(z-vt)). Here v is constant since the coefficients are not z or t dependent.

b) Since the sign of the velocity determines the propagation direction, and we have already identified that v = (b)/(a), the wave propagates in the positive (negative) direction on the z-axis when (b)/(a) > 0 ((b)/(a) < 0). The speed of the perturbation is then | (b)/(a)|.

c): The function represents a wave since, as mentioned after eq.(3.2.8) in the lecture notes, a function of the form ψ (z,t) = f(z± vt) is a wave if it is twice differentiable with respect to space and time.

II: ψ (z,t)=exp(-c|az-bt|+d) = exp(-c|a||z-(b)/(a)t|+d)

a): The function propagates at a constant velocity while maintaining its shape if a,b,c ≠ 0.

b): The speed of the perturbation is v = (b)/(a). The wave propagates in the positive (negative) direction on the z-axis when (b)/(a) > 0 ((b)/(a) < 0)

c): No, since the function is not twice differentiable at z = (b)/(a)t because the derivative of the absolute value function has a discontinuity at that point.

III: ψ (z,t)=cos(abz +cz²)

a): Under no conditions, since the function is not time-dependent.

b): No velocity, since no time-dependence.

c): No, since not twice differentiable with respect to time.

To solve Aₛ and εₛ using the complex notation, equation
can be edited to the form

Aₛ e^(i (φ+εₛ)) = A₁ e^(i φ)e^(i ε₁)+ A₂ e^(i φ)e^(iε₂) \
⇔ Aₛ e^(i φ) e^(i εₛ) = e^(i φ) (A₁ e^(i ε₁)+ A₂ e^(i ε₂))

⇔ Aₛ e^(i εₛ) = A₁ e^(i ε₁)+ A₂ e^(i ε₂) ,

where φ = kx-ω t. Recalling θ= atan (Im(z))/(Re(z)) = atan (y)/(x), we can write for the phase

εₛ = atan ((Im(A₁ e^(i ε₁)+ A₂ e^(i ε₂)))/(Re(A₁ e^(i ε₁)+ A₂ e^(i ε₂))))

⇒ εₛ = atan ((A₁ sinε₁ + A₂ sin ε₂)/(A₁ cosε₁ + A₂ cos ε₂)) .

By applying the law cosines to our problem, we get the following equation

Aₛ² = A₁² + A₂² - 2 A₁A₂ cos γ ,

where the angle γ should next be linked to the phases ε₁ and ε₂. After drawing an illustrating figure of the two complex numbers (vectors) in the complex plane, one see that the angles are related via γ = π -(ε₂-ε₁) = π -ε₂+ε₁. Inserting this into the above equation and noting the properties of the cosine function we find the sought form

Aₛ² = A₁² + A₂² + 2 A₁A₂ cos(ε₂ - ε₁) \
⇒ Aₛ = √(A₁² + A₂² + 2 A₁A₂ cos(ε₂ - ε₁)) .

=± i ê_(±).

b) The equation of motion for our situation is given as

mx⃗̈+mγx⃗̇+mω₀²x⃗=q(E⃗+v⃗×B⃗),

where B⃗=B₀ê_z and ω₀ = √(k/m).

We formulate an ansatz, assuming that the electron displacement follows the applied circularly polarized electric field E⃗=ê_(±)E₀e^(-i ω t), i.e., that x⃗=x₀e^(-i ω t)ê_(±). The first and second derivatives, i.e. velocity v and acceleration, become x⃗̇=-i ωx⃗ and x⃗̈=-ω²x⃗, respectively. By substituting these into Eq , we get that

-mω²x⃗-i mγωx⃗+mω₀²x⃗=q(E⃗-i ωx⃗×B⃗)

⇒ (-ω²-i γω+ω₀²)x⃗=(q)/(m)(E⃗-i ωx⃗×B⃗)

Let us consider now the cross-product term on the right-hand side. By using the result derived in a), we get that

x⃗̇×B⃗ = -i ωx⃗×B⃗=-i ω x₀e^(-i ω t)(ê_(±)×ê_z)B₀=-i ω x₀e^(-i ω t)B₀(± i ê_(±)) =±ω B₀x⃗.

We can substitute this to the Eq. and solve the form of x⃗ using the method shown in the lecture notes. First, we get that

(-ω²-i γω+∓ω B₀(q)/(m)+ω₀²)x⃗=(q)/(m)E⃗,

where the exponential terms of x⃗ and E⃗ cancel each other out, resulting in

x₀=(q)/(m)E₀(1)/(ω₀²-ω²-i γω∓(q)/(m)ω B₀)

and consequently

x⃗=(q)/(m)(1)/(ω₀²-ω²-i γω∓(q)/(m)ω B₀)E⃗.

The material polarization is given by P⃗=Nqx⃗ and also by P⃗=ε₀χ_(±)(ω)E⃗. By using the result in Eq. , we get that

(Nq²)/(m)(1)/(ω₀²-ω²-i γω∓(q)/(m)ω B₀)=ε₀χ_(±)(ω)

and finally that

2.4:
Maxwell's equations in isotropic and homogeneous material:

a) The macroscopic Maxwell's Equations are given as

∇·D⃗=ρ_f, ∇×E⃗=-∂(B⃗)/∂(t), ∇·B⃗=0, ∇×H⃗=J⃗_f+∂(D⃗)/∂(t).

Now, we assume that there are no free charges, free currents, and no material magnetization, i.e., ρ_f=0, J⃗_f=0, and M=0. Thus, the magnetic field becomes H⃗=B⃗/μ₀, while the electric displacement is given by D⃗=ε₀E⃗+P⃗. Hence, we can write the Ampère's circuital law as

∇×B⃗=μ₀∂(D⃗)/∂(t)=μ₀[ε₀∂(E⃗)/∂(t)+∂(P⃗)/∂(t)].

The curl of the electric field is given by the Maxwell--Faraday law:

∇×E⃗=-∂(B⃗)/∂(t).

By taking the curl of Eq. and noting that operators ∇× and ∂()/∂(t) commute for well behaved functions (i.e. ∇×∂()/∂(t)=∂()/∂(t)∇×, see the lecture notes), we get

∇×∇×E⃗=∇×(-∂(B⃗)/∂(t))=-∂()/∂(t)(∇×B⃗).

To the equation above, we can apply Eq. and get

∇×∇×E⃗=-μ₀ε₀∂²(E⃗)/∂(t)²-μ₀∂²(P⃗)/∂(t)².

For magnetic flux B⃗, we get from Eq. , using the distributive law for the curl operation

∇×∇×B⃗ =∇×(μ₀[ε₀∂(E⃗)/∂(t)+∂(P⃗)/∂(t)])

=μ₀ε₀∂()/∂(t)∇×E⃗+μ₀∂()/∂(t)∇×P⃗,

and finally, with Eq. that

∇×∇×B⃗=-μ₀ε₀∂²(B⃗)/∂(t)²+μ₀∂()/∂(t)∇×P⃗
.

b) We recall the identity ∇×∇×F⃗=∇(∇·F⃗)-∇²F⃗. Thus, we can rewrite Eq. and solve for the Laplacian of the electric field as

∇(∇·E⃗)-∇²E⃗=-μ₀ε₀∂²(E⃗)/∂(t)²-μ₀∂²(P⃗)/∂(t)²

⇒ ∇²E⃗=μ₀ε₀∂²(E⃗)/∂(t)²+μ₀∂²(P⃗)/∂(t)²-∇(∇·E⃗).

Since ∇·D⃗=ρ_f and D⃗=εE⃗, the divergence in an isotropic medium with no free charges or currents is zero (∇·E⃗=0). Additionally, the material polarization is given by P⃗=ε₀χE⃗. Thus, we can then rewrite the equation as

∇²E⃗=μ₀ε₀∂²(E⃗)/∂(t)²+μ₀ε₀χ∂²(E⃗)/∂(t)²=μ₀ε₀(1+χ)∂²(E⃗)/∂(t)².

The equation above is in the form of a typical wave equation. From the equation, we recognize the inverse square of the speed of light in the medium:

(1)/(v²)=μ₀ε₀(1+χ)

⇒ v=(1)/(√(μ₀ε₀(1+χ)))=(1)/(√(μ₀ε₀)√(1+χ)).

The speed of light in vacuum is given by c₀=1/√(μ₀ε₀) and the refractive index n is defined through v=c₀/n. Thus, we can write that

n=(c₀)/(v)=√(1+χ).

c) A plane wave of form A exp (i k⃗· r⃗ -i ω t) = A exp (i n k⃗₀ · r⃗ -i ω t) solves the wave equation. Since the refractive index is given by n=√(1+χ), the complex-valued susceptibility turns n into a complex-valued function n = Re (n) +i Im (n) = Re (n) +i κ . Inserting this into our plane wave, we see that positive-valued imaginary part of χ turns the wave into an attenuating wave, while the negative-valued part turns the wave into an amplifying wave. Waves of first type can be found e.g. inside lossy media, while latter ones can be found inside gain materials (e.g. light amplification inside a laser crystal).

3.2:
a): Let P₁ = (0,0,z_P) lie on the z-axis, far away from the scatterers, so that ‖r_P‖ = R₁ can be treated as a common distance for every scatterer. Since all scatterers radiate with the same amplitude Aⱼ = A, and the wave vector k at P does not depend on the index j, the phase k·R = k·(r_P-rⱼ) reduces, on-axis, to k(z_P-zⱼ) = kz_P - kzⱼ. This combines with the extra propagation phase factor exp(ikzⱼ) that each scattered wavelet already carries (accounting for the phase accumulated by the incident wave in reaching scatterer j), so that the zⱼ-dependence cancels exactly:

E_(T) = ∑ⱼ₌₁^N A (exp❴ikz_P❵)/(R₁)exp(-ikzⱼ+ikzⱼ)exp(-iω t) \
= (Aexp❴ikz_P❵)/(R₁)exp(-iω t)∑ⱼ₌₁^(N)1 = NA (exp❴ikz_P❵)/(R₁)exp(-iω t) .

All N contributions therefore add up in phase, exactly as in ordinary constructive interference. The corresponding irradiance is

I_(P₁)∝ E_(T)E_(T)^(*) = N²A² (exp❴ikz_P❵)/(R₁)·(exp❴-ikz_P❵)/(R₁) = (N²A²)/(R₁²) ,

i.e. I_(P₁)∝ N²: along the axis, the scatterers act as a fully-phased (coherent) array.

b): Now consider an off-axis point P₂=(x_P,y_P,L), still with ‖r_P‖≈ R₂ approximately constant for all scatterers, but write the accumulated phase from the j-th scatterer to P₂ as φⱼ ≡ kₓx_P+k_yy_P+k_zzⱼ, so that

E_(T) = ∑ⱼ₌₁^(N) A (exp❴iφⱼ❵)/(R₂)exp(-iω t) .

The irradiance is then, introducing a second dummy index l (also running over the N scatterers) for the complex-conjugate sum,

I_(P₂)∝ E_(T)E_(T)^(*) = (A²)/(R₂²)[∑ⱼ₌₁^N exp❴iφⱼ❵][∑ₗ₌₁^Nexp❴-iφₗ❵] = (A²)/(R₂²)∑ⱼ₌₁^(N)∑ₗ₌₁^(N)exp❴i(φⱼ-φₗ)❵ .

Splitting the double sum into diagonal (j=l) and off-diagonal (j≠ l) terms gives

I_(P₂)∝ (A²)/(R₂²)∑ⱼ₌₁^(N)1_(= N) + (A²)/(R₂²)∑ⱼ₌₁^(N)∑_(l=1 \ l≠ j)^(N)exp❴i(φⱼ-φₗ)❵ .

The diagonal term is simply N, since each phase cancels against itself. In the cross term, the phase difference Δφ = φⱼ-φₗ depends on the (random) relative positions of scatterers j and l; for a spatially disordered ensemble it is effectively uniformly distributed over [-π,π]. The corresponding phasors exp❴iΔφ❵ therefore land at essentially random points on the unit circle in the complex plane, and for sufficiently large N their sum averages to zero. Hence

I_(P₂) ∝ N (A²)/(R₂²) ,

i.e. I_(P₂)∝ N.

Physically, parts a) and b) together illustrate a general feature of scattering from a disordered ensemble: a sharply-peaked, coherent (constructive-interference) response, scaling as N², is only obtained within a narrow range of observation directions -- here, along the axis on which the incident wave already propagates -- where the individual phases φⱼ happen to be (nearly) equal for every scatterer. In every other direction, the randomly varying relative phases wash out the interference term, and the total irradiance instead scales simply as N times the irradiance of a single scatterer, exactly as expected for N mutually incoherent sources. This is the same mechanism behind the strongly forward-peaked far-field scattering/diffraction pattern of a finite, disordered collection of scatterers, in contrast to the isotropic (N-independent) radiation pattern of a single point source.
3.3:
a): The Fresnel coefficient is given by

r_(⊥)=(Eᵣ)/(Eᵢ)=(nᵢ cos θᵢ-nₜ cos θₜ)/(nᵢ cos θᵢ+nₜ cos θₜ) ,

and the reflectivity as

R_⊥ = | r_(⊥) |² .

The above equations can be solved for the condition R_⊥ by taking use of the Snell's law we can solve for the transmission angle θₜ:

nₜ sin θₜ =nᵢ sin θᵢ

θₜ =arcsin ((nᵢ)/(nₜ) sin θᵢ) .

The above (transcendental) equations cannot be analytically solved, so we resort to solving them numerically. Simple matlab codes as below:

We find that angles θᵢ > 86.5^∘ ensure the sought reflectivity.

b): Let's first consider the geometry where N parallel glass slides are separated by thin air spaces in between them. A light source is observed through this stack along the normal (to the glass plates) direction. The system consists now of 2N interfaces (N interfaces are glass-to-air interfaces, while N interfaces are air-to-glass interfaces).

Let's assume that the magnitude of the electric field associated with the incident electromagnetic wave E_(in)=1. Also, let's assume that absorption is negligible. Let's say, t₁ is the transmission coefficient of the first air-to-glass interface. Using Fresnel's formula at I₁, we can write

t₁=(2 n_(air))/(nₐᵢᵣ+n_(glass)) .

Transmission coefficients from all odd-numbered interfaces i.e. air-to-glass interfaces should also be the same i.e. t₁=t₃=t₅=…=t_(2 N-1).

Now let's assume that t₂ is the transmission coefficient of the first glass-to-air interface. Using Fresnel's formula at I₂, we can write

t₂=(2 n_(glass))/(n_(glass)+n_(air)) .

Transmission coefficients from all even-numbered interfaces i.e. glass-to-air interfaces should also be the same i.e. t₂=t₄=t₆=…=t_(2 N).

Hence, the total transmission coefficient of the stack consisting of N microscope slides is

t_(Total)=[t₁ · t₃ · t₅ … t_(2 N-1)] ·[t₂ · t₄ · t₆ … t_(2 N)]=(t₁ · t₂) ·(t₃ · t₄) …(t_(2 N-1) · t_(2 N))=(t₁ · t₂)^(N) .

Hence, the total transmitted electric field is E_(out)=(t₁ · t₂)^(N). The total transmitted electric field intensity

Tₜ=Iₒᵤₜ=Eₒᵤₜ²=(t₁ · t₂)^(2 N) .

Putting n_(glass)=1.5 and n_(air)=1 in Eq. (4), we obtain

Tₜ=Iₒᵤₜ=(0.96)^(2 N) .

For a stack of five glass slides, N=5. Putting N=5 in Eq. (5), we obtain Tₜ=I_(out)= (0.96)¹⁰=0.665. Hence, for a stack of five glass slides, 66.5 % light will be transmitted.

The above attenuation factor (or more precisely 1-T) might seem irrelevant in terms of optical applications. However, it provides us an extremely valuable rule of thumb to estimate performances of optical instrument, that often consist of several glass components (lenses, prisms, protective windows etc.). Already five components reduce the transmitted signal strength to around 66 %, quickly motivating to move from uncoated optical components to anti-reflection coated ones. An interested reader is referred to our course on optical thin films.

In addition, it is often useful to reduce the number of air–glass/glass–air interfaces by gluing components, such as lenses, into each other. Carl Zeiss' Tessar lens is a good example of this trick.

c) The Brewster's angle condition is given by

θᵢ+θₜ=90^(∘) ,

which can be inserted into the Snell's law to give the angle

θₚ=arctan ((nₜ)/(nᵢ)) =arctan ((1.5)/(1)) = 56.3 deg.

d) Provided that incident light is well collimated (i.e. close to a plane wave), and propagating inside the thin glass plate at large enough incidence angles, light can be totally internally reflected at the glass--air interfaces (θᵢ > θ_(c)=arcsin (n₂ / n₁). When this happens, all of incident light is reflected at the interfaces, and the plate starts to act as a one-dimensional waveguide. Note, that the waveguide doesn't trap light along the direction parallel to the interface, i.e. light will diverge/spread out along this direction upon long enough propagation distances.

4.4:
a) We start by writing equations (based on the given figure) for the circulating, round-trip and launched fields:

E_(circ) =E_(launch)+E_(RT)

E_(RT) =r₁ r₂ e^(i φ) E_(circ)

E_(launch) =t₁ E_(inc)

which can be used to solve the ratio of interest

(E_(circ))/(E_ inc) = (t₁ · E_(circ))/(E_ launch) = (t₁)/(1 - r₁ r₂ e^(-i φ))

allowing us to calculate the asked enhancement factor by taking the squared modulus of above ratio resulting in

A_(circ) = | (E_(circ))/(E_ inc) |² = | (t₁)/(1 - r₁ r₂ e^(-i φ)) |² .

b) Next, we want to simplify the derived enhancement factor by considering a case where our incident light is exactly on resonance with the enhancement cavity. In this case, φ = 2 π m, where m is an integer, resulting in the exponent to be equal to unity.

Recalling that at normal incidence the reflection (transmission) coefficients are related to reflectivity (transmissivity) via Rᵢ = | rᵢ |² (Tᵢ = | tᵢ |²), the equation turns into

A_(circ) = | (E_(circ))/(E_ inc) |² = (T₁)/((1 - r₁ r₂)²) = (T₁)/((1 - √(R₁ R₂))²) .

c) This is a straightforward calculation where one can easily find the right values by using simple matlab/python codes (e.g. use interp1-function). The reflectivities R₁ were found to be 0.9609, 0.9922 and 0.9962. Interestingly, I had trouble calculating the last value with co-pilot.

d) Finally, let's show that the enhancement factor A'ₜᵣₐₙₛ(φ) ≡ (Iₜᵣₐₙₛ)/(I_(inc)) is of form A'ₜᵣₐₙₛ(φ) = (1-R₁)(1-R₂) A_(circ), where A_(circ) ≡ (I_(circ))/(I_(launch)).

In case it's not yet clear, e.g. co-pilot can essentially solve the problem for you. Launched field is of form:

E_(launch)=t₁ E_(inc) ⇒ I_(launch)= T₁ I_(inc)=(1-R₁) I_(inc) ,

where we have assumed the mirror 1 to be non-absorptive and non-scattering, thus fulfilling R₁ + T₁ = 1.

The same algebra works for the field transmitted through the second mirror:

E_(trans)=t₂ E_(circ) ⇒ I_(trans)=T₂ I_(circ)=(1-R₂) I_(circ) .

Using the definition for A_(circ), we can write for the transmitted irradiance:

I_(trans)=(1-R₂) A_(circ) · I_(launch) ,

which gives us, after another substitution (I_(launch)=(1-R₁) I_(inc)), the ratio of interest:

A'ₜᵣₐₙₛ = (I_(trans))/(I_(inc)) =(1-R₂) (1-R₁) A_(circ) .

5.4:
We consider a circular aperture with radius a. The circ-function is defined as circ(r′) = 1, for 0 ≤ r′ < 1 and zero otherwise. Likewise, circ(r/a) = 1, for 0 ≤ r/a < 1 (or equally 0 ≤ r < a) and zero otherwise for an aperture with radius a.
Thus, the normalized, unitless amplitude in the diffraction integral can be written as E_A(r) = circ(r/a), or equally E_A(x,y) = circ(√(x²+y²)/a).

As the circ-function is given for a radius of 1, it is convenient to change the coordinates x and y to normalized coordinates x′ = x/a and y' = y/a. Hence, the integration variable needs to be changed as well: d x′/d x = 1/a ⇒ d x = ad x′.

The Fraunhofer diffraction integral was given by

Eₜₒₜ(X,Y) ≈ (e^(i kR))/(R) ∬_S E_A(x,y) e^(-i k(Xx+Yy)/R) d x d y.

Let's substitute to the above the normalized coordinates and the E_A. We get

Eₜₒₜ(X,Y) ≈ (e^(i kR))/(R) ∬_(-∞)^∞ circ(√(x^(′ 2)+y^(′ 2))) exp(-i(ka)/(R)(Xx′+Yy′)) a² d x′ d y′

= (e^(i kR))/(R) a² ∬_(-∞)^∞ circ(√(x^(′ 2)+y^(′ 2))) e^(-i (νₓx′+ν_yy′)) d x′ d y′

= (e^(i kR))/(R) a² (2π J₁(√(νₓ²+ν_y²)))/(√(νₓ²+ν_y²)),

where νₓ = akX/R and ν_y = akY/R. The last step utilizes the given Fourier transform of the circ-function.

Let's next calculate the irradiance

I(X,Y) ∝ |Eₜₒₜ(X,Y)|² = EₜₒₜEₜₒₜ^* = (a⁴)/(R²) [ (2π J₁(√(νₓ²+ν_y²)))/(√(νₓ²+ν_y²)) ]²

= (π²a⁴)/(R²) [ (2J₁(√((akX/R)²+(akY/R)²)))/(√((akX/R)²+(akY/R)²)) ]².

Lastly, we will change the coordinates to cylindrical coordinates where q is the radius and q² = X² + Y². The irradiance now becomes of the familiar form

I(q) = I₀ (π²a⁴)/(R²) [ (2J₁(√((akq/R)²))/(√((akq/R)²)) ]²
= I(0) [(2J₁(akq/R))/((akq/R)) ]²,

where I(0) = I₀(π²a⁴)/(R²) and I₀ is a constant dependent on the irradiance of the input plane wave.

6.3:
Solution 1:
We start by writing down the Snell's law:

n sin θᵢ = nₐᵢᵣ sin θₜ = sin θₜ ,

where we aim to describe the sine terms using the parameters n, R and h. The sine (and cosine) of θᵢ are easily found by looking at the given figure

sin θᵢ = (h)/(R) , cos θᵢ = (R-d)/(R)

We then focus on the θₜ term, where a relation for the relevant angles can be found, again, by carefully looking at the figure:

(π)/(2)-θᵢ+γ+θₜ = π ⇒ θₜ = (π)/(2)-γ+θᵢ .

The above relation enables us to write for the sine of θₜ a relation

sin θₜ = sin ((π)/(2) - γ + θᵢ) = cos (γ -θᵢ) ,

which can be cast into a useful form by recalling the trigonometric identity of

cos (γ- θᵢ)=cos γ cos θᵢ +sin γ sin θᵢ ,

where the γ terms can be written out as (using the geometry of the situation)

sin γ=(f+d)/(√((f+d)²+h²)) , cos γ=(h)/(√((f+d)²+h²)) .

Using Eqs. and the above equation can now by written as

sin θₜ = cos γ cos θᵢ +sin γ sin θᵢ

= (h)/(√((f+d)²+h²)) (R-d)/(R) +(f+d)/(√((f+d)²+h²)) (h)/(R)

= (h)/(√((f+d)²+h²)) (R-d)/(R) +(f+d)/(√((f+d)²+h²)) (h)/(R)

= (h)/(R) (R+f)/(√((f+d)²+h²)) .

The Snell's law now turns into

n (h)/(R)= (h)/(R) (R+f)/(√((f+d)²+h²)) ⇒ n √((f+d)²+h²)= R+f ,

where d can be found out to be (again, from figure)

(R-d)² +h² = R² ⇒ d=R-√(R²-h²) .

Looking at the above form for d, we can verify the length to be very small. Since in practise the radii of curvatures for lenses R are far greater than the beam heights h, the length

d=R-√(R²-h²) = R-R√(1-(h²)/(R²)) ≈ R-R (1-(h²)/(2R²)) = (h²)/(2R²) ,

which is indeed a small number, since h ≪ R. We can therefore safely conclude that (d+f)² ≈ f², allowing us to solve the above equation into

n² (f+d)²+n² h² = (R+f)²

n² f² +n²h² = R² + 2Rf + f²

(n²-1) f² -2Rf +n²h²-R² = 0 ,

which is a quadratic equation that can be solved using the celebrated quadratic formula
After some straightforward algebra (and recalling that d ≪ f, i.e. (d+f)² ≈ f²), the focal length is found to be approximately

f(h, n, R) = (2R ± √(4R² - 4 (n²-1) (n²h²-R²)))/(2(n²-1)) ,

f(h, n, R) = (2R ± 2√(R² - n⁴ h² +n² h² +n² R² -R²))/(2(n²-1)) ,

f(h, n, R) = (R ± √(n² (h²-n²h² + R²)))/(n²-1)

f(h, n, R) = (R ± n√(h²(1-n²) + R²))/(n²-1)

f(h, n, R) = (R ± n√(R² -h²(n²-1)))/(n²-1)

which despite its slight complexity tells us that the focal position f indeed depends on the height h (in addition to n and R). We also see that the focal length decreases when h increases, and furthermore can resolve the usual relation for the focal length, familiar upon working under the paraxial approximation (h ≈ 0, and we neglect the negative-valued solution for f):

f(0, n, R) ≈ (R+nR)/((n+1)(n-1)) = (R(1+n))/((n+1)(n-1)) = (R)/(n-1) .

The optical paths are illustrated in Fig. 2. There are a total of 7 variables including the focal length f, the length of the optical system L, separation of the lenses in the two positions d, and the object and image distances for the two positions (referred with subscripts 1 and 2). On the other hand, there are 6 equations that we can construct (3 pairs): 2 for L, 2 for d, and 2 for f

L=sₒ₁+sᵢ₁=sₒ₂+sᵢ₂.

d=sᵢ₁-sᵢ₂=sₒ₂-sₒ₁.

(1)/(f)=(1)/(sₒ₁)+(1)/(sᵢ₁)=(1)/(sₒ₂)+(1)/(sᵢ₂).

Now, we are ready for a process of solving for f with respect to d and L. We start from Eq. (13). Using Eq. (11) in Eq. (13), we can write-

(1)/(f)=(1)/(sₒ₁)+(1)/(sᵢ₁)=(1)/(sₒ₁)+(1)/(L-sₒ₁).

(1)/(f)=(1)/(sₒ₂)+(1)/(sᵢ₂)=(1)/(sₒ₂)+(1)/(L-sₒ₂).

Using Eq. (12) in Eq. (15), we get

(1)/(f)=(1)/(sₒ₂)+(1)/(sᵢ₂)=(1)/(sₒ₂)+(1)/(L-sₒ₂)=(1)/(d+sₒ₁)+(1)/(L-(d+sₒ₁)).

Now, we solve for sₒ₁ from Eqs. (14) and (16).

(1)/(sₒ₁)+(1)/(L-sₒ₁)=(1)/(d+sₒ₁)+(1)/(L-d-sₒ₁),

(L-sₒ₁+sₒ₁)/(sₒ₁(L-sₒ₁))=(L-d-sₒ₁+d+sₒ₁)/((d+sₒ₁)(L-d-sₒ₁)).

sₒ₁L-sₒ₁²=dL-d²-dsₒ₁+sₒ₁L-dsₒ₁-sₒ₁²,

0=dL-d²-2dsₒ₁.

sₒ₁=(dL-d²)/(2d)=(L-d)/(2).

We now replace sₒ₁ from Eq. (21) into Eq. (14) to get

(1)/(f)=(1)/((L-d)/2)+(1)/(L-(L-d)/2)=(2)/(L-d)+(2)/(L+d)=(4L)/(L²-d²),

f=(L²-d²)/(4L).

This is the mathematical expression of the focal length of the lens involving the ﬁxed length L and the measured distance d.
The same solution can also be derived by looking at the two solutions to the quadratic equation

(1)/(f)=(1)/(sₒ)+(1)/(L-s₀) rightarrow sₒ²-Lsₒ+Lf = 0.

It is also noteworthy that the two lens positions obey the condition

(s₀₂)/(s₀₁) = (sᵢ₁)/(sᵢ₂),

which is fulfilled, in the present scenario, when sₒ₂ = sᵢ₁ and sₒ₁ = sᵢ₂.
As for the limitations on the focal length that can be measured, we consider a limiting situation when d→ 0. In this case the two solutions for the problem would merge into one and we get

f=(L²)/(4L)=(L)/(4).

This is the longest focal length that can be measured with this setup. Mathematically, there is no real lower limit for the shortest focal length that can be measured. However, experimentally, the size of the image would get inﬁnitely large or the object would need to be inﬁnitely large so there could be some limitations. In addition, the lenses to produce very small focal lengths are far from ideal thin lenses.
